front: Why were there concerns about Edward VI's age in 1547?
p1: Edward only 9 → feared a regent might seize power, as Richard III had done in his nephew's minority in 1483.
p2: A 9-year-old boy could not project the image of a divinely appointed, just, military monarch.
p3: Henry left a divided council — Gardiner and Norfolk's fall in 1546 already weighted it to reformists → Edward couldn't control faction.

front: How did Somerset gain and use power?
p1: Seymour conspired with Paget → used the dry stamp and 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will → made himself Duke of Somerset and Lord Protector.
p2: Ruled as an autocrat from Somerset House. Centralised power against Henry's will of 16 co-equal councillors. Denied Edward any role — and pocket money.
p3: Positioned himself as the Good Duke — ally of the ordinary man and religious reformer. Led forces against Scotland in the Rough Wooing.

front: How dangerous was faction under Somerset?
p1: In a minority, no authority to control faction → disputes could spill into rebellion or civil war.
p2: Somerset gave positions to supporters including his brother Thomas Seymour — later executed for attempting a coup → dangerous culture of ambition.
p3: Anti-Somerset Faction: reformers and conservatives — Warwick, Wriothesley, Paget. Former allies now united against him.

front: Why did Somerset fall from power in October 1549?
p1: Anti-Somerset faction (Warwick, Wriothesley, Paget) blamed his arrogant leadership for the unrest of 1549.
p2: Feeling threatened → Somerset issued a general summons on 5th October for loyal subjects to defend him against the Council. Seen as inciting revolt.
p3: Retreated to Windsor Castle → surrendered when the King turned against him, declaring he was being kept prisoner.

front: How did Northumberland consolidate power after Somerset's fall?
p1: Facing conservative opposition, Warwick allied with reformists → committed to further religious reform. Lord President of the Council 1550; Duke of Northumberland.
p2: Released Somerset in 1550 hoping to use him as an ally. When this failed → Somerset executed 1552 on likely fabricated treason charges.
p3: Worked more closely with Edward VI — involved him in government. Knew maintaining the monarch's support was crucial.

front: Why did Northumberland and Edward attempt to alter the succession in 1553?
p1: Edward feared for his Protestant changes — Mary was a committed Catholic who refused even his personal appeals to convert.
p2: Northumberland feared his own fall when Mary came to the throne → married son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey to control the heir.
p3: Edward's illness progressed before Jane Grey had children → in his own hand he crossed out 'male heirs' and named Jane Grey directly, giving the Devise a shaky legal basis.

front: Why did the Devise for the Succession fail to prevent Mary's accession?
p1: Mary had a power base in East Anglia — significant hatred of Northumberland after Kett's Rebellion → proclaimed herself Queen 9th July, before the Council's proclamation of Jane on 10th.
p2: Council never truly believed in the Devise — bullied into it by Northumberland. Army deserted him on the march north; councillors broke ranks for Mary → retreated to Cambridge, accepted Mary on 19th.
p3: Mary entered London to rousing popular support → popular legitimacy proved more powerful than legal manoeuvring. Northumberland, Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley all executed.

front: Why did Mary's gender create problems for her rule?
p1: First Queen to rule in her own right — many believed female rulers could not: control powerful men; lead armies; project monarchical strength. Precedent: Matilda's claim → civil war in 12th century.
p2: John Knox, The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558) — compared female rulers to 'the blind leading those who can see'.
p3: Marriage a serious hurdle — wife expected to obey husband. Serious consequences whether Mary married an English noble or a foreign prince.

front: How far did Mary's gender actually undermine her authority as queen?
p1: Despite fears, Mary managed her Council effectively — faction less serious under Mary than under Edward.
p2: During Wyatt's Rebellion, stayed in London against Council's advice → delivered Guildhall speech to rally Londoners. Female ruler could act with decisive strength.
p3: Willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen shows gender mattered less than religion — concerns about female rule were subordinate to other calculations.

front: Why was Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain controversial?
p1: Foreign marriage risked: influx of foreigners; entanglement in foreign wars; xenophobic popular reaction → Wyatt's Rebellion broke out January 1554, ostensibly in reaction.
p2: Philip: Mary's personal choice, championed by Paget. Father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor → powerful Habsburg alliance. English alternative: Edward Courtenay, championed by Gardiner.
p3: Ended unhappily — after Mary's phantom pregnancy, Philip rarely visited England. On her death he noted he felt 'a reasonable regret'.

front: How was the marriage to Philip designed to limit its dangers?
p1: Treaty agreed: Philip named King but with no power in his own right. No Spaniards to receive offices or English lands.
p2: After Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne. England not to be drawn into Spain's wars.
p3: Treaty ultimately failed — England drawn into Spain's war with France → humiliating loss of Calais 1558, last English territory in France.

front: How effectively did Mary manage faction on her Privy Council?
p1: Casual councillors excluded from key committees 1554. Inner council established 1555 — only most valued advisors present.
p2: Three key figures: Gardiner (cautious realist); Paget (exceptional administrator); Cardinal Pole (zealous Catholic). Pole's return 1554 → dispute with Gardiner over pace of restoration.
p3: Struggles minor and short-lived — Gardiner's death 1555 ended moderating influence. For most of the reign the Council worked effectively and carried out Mary's wishes.

front: How smooth was the succession of 1558?
p1: Mary died having failed to produce an heir. On her deathbed, reluctantly recognised Elizabeth as successor — asked her to preserve the Catholic faith.
p2: Philip of Spain chose not to press his claim — preferred a Protestant England to a France-aligned Catholic one.
p3: Henry II of France proclaimed Mary Queen of Scots the true Queen of England → modified Mary Stuart's heraldry to include the English coat of arms.

front: What did Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession and will establish?
p1: 1543 Third Act of Succession: if Edward died without heirs → throne to Mary, then Elizabeth. Illegitimacy of both never reversed.
p2: Henry instructed a Regency Council of 16 members, balanced between reformists (Seymour) and conservatives (Gardiner and Norfolk).
p3: 'Unfulfilled gifts' clause → allowed Seymour and Paget to conspire and make Seymour Lord Protector, against Henry's wishes.

front: Who were the two candidates for Mary's hand in marriage and why was the choice controversial?
p1: Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon — championed by Gardiner as a powerful English noble with royal blood who would secure Mary's reign.
p2: Philip of Spain — championed by Paget and Mary's personal choice. Father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor — but risked xenophobic reaction.
p3: English noble → division and faction at court. Foreign prince → entanglement in foreign wars. No easy answer.

front: Who were the three key figures on Mary's Privy Council?
p1: Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester — committed Catholic and cautious realist. Imprisoned by Edward in 1551.
p2: William Paget — eminent political survivor and exceptional administrator. Served Henry, Edward and Mary. Not committed to religious change.
p3: Cardinal Reginald Pole — zealous Catholic returned from exile. Dispute with Gardiner over pace of restoration → Gardiner stressed caution; Pole favoured persecution.

front: What religious inheritance did Edward VI receive from Henry VIII?
p1: Henry never truly embraced Protestantism — only embraced changes that brought money and power, especially the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
p2: 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic practices: Transubstantiation; clerical celibacy. England doctrinally Catholic despite break with Rome.
p3: Outside London and East Anglia, the majority just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium — didn't understand differences between Catholicism and Protestantism.

front: What did the three stages of the Edwardian Reformation achieve?
p1: Stage 1 — Destruction 1547: iconoclasm encouraged; Six Articles and Treason Act repealed; Chantries dissolved. Old had to be destroyed before new installed.
p2: Stage 2 — Limbo 1548–49: First Book of Common Prayer — deliberately vague on Communion, pleased nobody → prompted the Western Rebellion. Repeal of Treason Laws → radical preaching unleashed.
p3: Stage 3 — Formulation 1550–53: Second Book of Common Prayer (1552) removed all Catholic practices; Communion purely symbolic. Forty-Two Articles drafted but Edward died before passing — 1553.

front: How far was England Protestant by 1553?
p1: De jure England was Protestant — de facto very doubtful. Six years not enough to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship.
p2: Bishop Hooper's visitations: of 311 Gloucester clergymen, 171 couldn't recite the Ten Commandments; 40 couldn't find the Lord's Prayer.
p3: Evidence from wills: little support for changes outside London and East Anglia. Rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary → traditional religion retained its popularity.

front: What were Mary's religious aims and why were they difficult to achieve?
p1: Aims: undo all religious changes since 1529 — restore Papal authority, Catholic practices, Transubstantiation, dissolved monasteries. Secure future by marrying and producing an heir.
p2: Advisors cautious: Gardiner doubted restoring Papal authority; Renard warned against rushing monastic property; even Charles V and the Pope urged caution.
p3: Parliament refused to repeal the Act of Supremacy October 1553. April 1554 — landowning MPs refused to reinstate heresy laws until Mary guaranteed ex-monastic land was safe.

front: What was the process of Mary's Counter-Reformation?
p1: First Act of Repeal (1553) reversed Edward's changes immediately. Royal Injunctions 1554 restored Catholic practices — Holy Days, processions, ceremonies → large numbers of married clergy deprived.
p2: Second Act of Repeal (November 1554) repealed all religious legislation since 1529. Compromise forced on ex-monastic land — not restored to the Church.
p3: Pole's 12 Decrees 1556 banned absenteeism, pluralism and simony → improving clerical quality, not just restoring Catholicism.

front: Why were the Marian burnings counter-productive?
p1: 284 burned (51 women), mostly in Protestant strongholds of the south-east. Large crowds attended but little evidence burnings converted anyone — many viewed them as entertainment.
p2: Burnings of prominent Protestant bishops inspired resistance. Cranmer's burning 1556: plunged the hand that signed his recantation into the flames first.
p3: ~800 Protestants fled abroad, including many printers → underground propaganda movement keeping Cranmer's Prayer Book and Foxe's Book of Martyrs in circulation, radicalising exiles with Calvinist ideas.

front: How far had England returned to Catholicism by 1558?
p1: Edward's short reign meant much of the country — especially the North — had always remained Catholic. Catholic worship returned speedily; Mary faced no rebellion purely on the issue of religion.
p2: Mary failed to suppress the Protestant underground. Two-thirds of printers were Protestant; 19,000 copies of the Second Book of Common Prayer remained in circulation alongside Foxe's Book of Martyrs.
p3: Failure to produce an heir → Catholicism did not triumph. But the time it took Elizabeth to re-establish Protestantism suggests the Marian restoration achieved significant de facto change.

front: What happened in Stage 1 — Destruction (1547) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: Royal injunctions issued → iconoclasm encouraged in churches across England.
p2: Six Articles repealed → removed Catholic doctrine set by Henry. Treason Act repealed → no longer treason to preach dissenting religious views.
p3: Chantries dissolved — seen as superstitious Catholic worship. Also brought in revenue and land for the Crown.

front: What happened in Stage 2 — Limbo (1548–49) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: Repeal of Treason Laws opened a Pandora's Box → Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism all preached, creating confusion about official doctrine.
p2: Cranmer's First Book of Common Prayer (December 1548) — enforced by First Act of Uniformity. Deliberately vague on Holy Communion → pleased nobody.
p3: Some Protestant practices encouraged but many Catholic survivals remained — e.g. belief in Purgatory. Iconoclasm repeatedly encouraged.

front: What happened in Stage 3 — Formulation (1550–53) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: New ordinal (1550) → leading Catholic clergy replaced with Protestants. New Treason Act: questioning the Royal Supremacy now an offence.
p2: Second Book of Common Prayer (1552) — far more radical: all Catholic practices removed; Communion confirmed as purely symbolic.
p3: Forty-Two Articles (1552) drew up key doctrines — never passed by Parliament before Edward died 1553. De jure England was Protestant by 1553; de facto another matter.

front: What were the main causes of the Great Price Rise in the mid-Tudor period?
p1: Population: Malthusian Crisis — rose from 2.3 to 3 million 1525–51. Agricultural productivity couldn't keep pace; bad harvests worsened by the Little Ice Age → food prices rose.
p2: Debasement: Henry VIII reduced precious metal content of coinage to fund wars → prices rose to compensate. Somerset continued debasement for the Scottish war, worsening inflation.
p3: Enclosure: arable → livestock farming for cloth market → less food, more unemployment. Commonwealth men blamed enclosure and greedy landlords for rack renting and regrating.

front: How far did Somerset's response to socioeconomic problems make the situation worse?
p1: Somerset commissioned John Hales to investigate enclosures 1548, imposed 5% Sheep Tax → raised expectations he could not fulfil.
p2: Vagrancy Act 1547: two years slavery for a first offence; lifetime slavery for a second. Deeply unpopular — instinct was punishment, not relief.
p3: Government fundamentally misunderstood the causes of the Great Price Rise beyond enclosure. Debasement continued to fund Scottish war in ignorance of its inflationary impact.

front: How serious was the wider unrest of 1549?
p1: 1549 — 'year of the many-headed monster': unrest in over half of English counties, the most widespread of the Tudor period. Kett's captured Norwich; Western Rebellion besieged Exeter for a month.
p2: Thousands of soldiers diverted from the Scottish border. The order to execute 3,000 Western rebels demonstrates the establishment's fear.
p3: Neither rebellion marched on London — demands written politely to Somerset; anger directed at local gentry rather than the Crown. No match for government force.

front: What were the causes of Kett's Rebellion?
p1: Began when a mob attacked enclosures of John Flowerdew, who redirected the protest to Robert Kett — a gentleman who had himself enclosed land, somehow became the rebellion's leader.
p2: Demands centred on: enclosure and high rents; absent or uneducated clergy. Written politely to Somerset, assuming his support as the Good Duke.
p3: In Norfolk, 6% owned 60% of the land → reflected genuine extreme economic inequality, not just political opportunism.

front: What happened during Kett's Rebellion?
p1: 16,000 rebels met July 1549 → marched on Norwich, camped at Mousehold Heath, stormed the city. Somerset's enclosure commissions had raised hopes he championed the poor.
p2: Kett's camp well-disciplined and organised — Kett maintained order and dispensed justice. No attempt made to march on London.
p3: Warwick arrived with 12,000 troops from the Scottish war → massacred rebels at Dussindale. 3,000 killed; 49 leaders executed for treason.

front: What were the causes of the Western Rebellion of 1549?
p1: Resistance to Protestant reforms. William Body murdered 1548 for overseeing iconoclasm in Helston. Cornishmen more familiar with Latin than English.
p2: Demands almost entirely religious — drawn up by literate local clergy. Dismissed new mass as a 'Christmas game'. 'Kill all the gentlemen!' chanted at Bodmin — economic grievances also present.
p3: West Country resentment of central government. Cornish viewed themselves as a distinct culture, language and nation. 1497 Cornish rebellion had been crushed by Henry VII.

front: What happened during the Western Rebellion?
p1: Rebels besieged Exeter for a month; attacked gentry at St Michael's Mount, Bodmin and Trematon Castle. Local militia failed to suppress revolt.
p2: Government forces of 8,000 led by Lord John Russell defeated rebels at Sampford Courtenay — over 3,000 executed.
p3: Failed due to lack of clear leadership — different sections attacked different targets, unlike the more organised Kett's Rebellion. Cornish language suppressed after the rebellion.

front: What were the causes of Wyatt's Rebellion in 1554?
p1: Ostensible cause: Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain — xenophobic fears over a foreign marriage; Spanish patronage; entanglement in Habsburg wars.
p2: Xenophobia may have masked other causes. Rebellion began in Protestant Kent — part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth. Many leaders had lost positions at court due to their faith.
p3: Collapse of the cloth trade → unemployment in Kent. Kentish people also had a long history of rebellion: 1381 and 1450.

front: How serious a threat was Wyatt's Rebellion to Mary's reign?
p1: Government soldiers deserted Norfolk and joined Wyatt declaring 'We are all Englishmen!' — Wyatt reached the gates of London. If Londoners had opened the city gates, the rebellion could have succeeded.
p2: Courtenay revealed the plot to Gardiner → forced Wyatt's hand too early, in January. French support and the other three rebel forces never materialised. Hard to sustain in winter.
p3: Mary's decisive Guildhall speech secured London's loyalty → gates stayed shut. Wyatt and leaders executed; Elizabeth imprisoned in the Tower but released after Wyatt refused to implicate her under torture.

front: How serious was the challenge of getting the Religious Settlement through Parliament?
p1: Catholic bishops and lay nobles in the Lords threatened to block the settlement — particularly objecting to making Elizabeth 'Head of the Church'.
p2: Elizabeth prorogued Parliament over Easter 1559, arrested two vocal critics — the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester → compromised: adopted 'Supreme Governor' instead.
p3: Settlement passed the Lords by just three votes. Marian bishops then removed when they refused to swear the Oath of Loyalty.

front: How did Puritans attempt to change the Religious Settlement through Parliament?
p1: 1571: Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer — remove vestments and kneeling. Summoned before the Privy Council for infringing Royal Prerogative → barred from Parliament.
p2: 1586: Anthony Cope MP made radical 'bill and book' proposal — replace Book of Common Prayer with Genevan Prayer Book; remove the episcopacy → Cope and four supporters sent to the Tower.
p3: J.E. Neale argued Cope and Strickland were part of an organised 'Puritan Choir' — a vocal, powerful precursor to the Puritan-dominated Parliament of the 17th century. Challenged by Elton.

front: How did Puritans challenge the settlement from within the Church?
p1: Vestiarian Controversy: Puritans despised vestments. Parker's 1566 Advertisements compromised — but 37 clergy who refused lost their jobs.
p2: Puritans attempted to alter the 39 Articles in Convocation (1563) — Anglican articles only passed by one vote. Ceremony left more ambiguous; doctrine clearly moderate.
p3: Bottom-up prophesying and classis movements 1570s–80s → tried to spread Calvinist and Presbyterian ideals among clergy. Later suppressed by Whitgift.

front: How did Puritans challenge the settlement through popular appeals?
p1: Cartwright gave Presbyterian lectures at Cambridge 1570 denouncing Church hierarchy → lost his professorship.
p2: Field and Wilcox published the Admonition to Parliament (1572) calling for end of episcopacy. Marprelate Tracts (1588–89) made vicious attacks on bishops — but alienated moderates.
p3: Separatist movements suppressed: Robert Browne's 1581 Brownist Church in Norwich; Barrow and Greenwood's 1590s movement → leaders arrested and executed 1593.

front: Why was the Catholic threat limited in the first decade of Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Elizabeth's tolerance: sole recusancy punishment was a 1 shilling fine. Many Church Papists attended CoE services before secret Catholic ones. Elizabeth 'would not open windows unto men's souls'.
p2: Philip of Spain persuaded Pope Pius IV not to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563 — Philip feared France gaining control of England if Mary Queen of Scots came to the throne.
p3: Elizabeth resisted Parliament's attempts to increase punishments. Law stated those refusing the Oath of Supremacy twice could be executed → Elizabeth decreed no one would be asked twice.

front: How did seminary priests and Jesuits transform the Catholic threat from the 1570s?
p1: William Allen's English College at Douai trained seminary priests — arriving in England from 1574. By 1585, 279 had travelled to England.
p2: From 1580s Jesuits also arrived — ~650 in total, sheltered by Catholic gentry in priest holes.
p3: Undermined Elizabeth's goal for Catholicism to 'wither on the vine'. New generation of priests revitalising the religion — network of priest holes particularly threatening.

front: What problems faced the Catholics 1559-1589?
p1: Government legislation effective. Initial tolerance → majority of Catholics conformed. Later reprisals and executions broadly effective.
p2: Foreign support weak. 1570 excommunication too little, too late. Habsburg-Valois rivalry prevented coordinated Catholic action until late 1580s. Armada failure (1588) → major propaganda boost for Protestantism.
p3: Elizabeth's 45-year reign was decisive — the Catholic establishment from Mary's reign died out; new generation of gentry, nobility and clergy grew up entirely under the Settlement.

front: What domestic religious pressures did Elizabeth face in 1558?
p1: Returning Marian exiles radicalised by Calvinist and Zwinglian ideas in Zurich, Frankfurt and Geneva — denied any role for the monarch in the Church.
p2: Powerful bishops Elizabeth inherited from Mary were all Catholics. Approximately one-third of the powerful English nobility and gentry retained the Catholic faith privately.
p3: Elizabeth's personal beliefs: raised Protestant but found radical Protestantism tedious — had a fondness for ceremonial aspects of Catholicism.

front: What international religious pressures did Elizabeth face in 1558?
p1: Spain and France both strongly Catholic. Habsburg-Valois rivalry kept them despising each other — Elizabeth's political future depended on that rivalry continuing.
p2: Scotland: Mary Queen of Scots married to the French Dauphin Francis. Henry II of France presented Mary as true Queen of England → a figure unifying Scotland, France and England against Elizabeth.
p3: Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce. In 1559 Scottish Protestant Lords overthrew Mary of Guise → Scotland became Protestant.

front: What were the key provisions of the Act of Supremacy (1559)?
p1: Removed the Pope's authority over the English Church. Made Elizabeth Supreme Governor — not 'Supreme Head' (Henry's title), to avoid offending those who believed a woman could not be head of the Church.
p2: Elizabeth in charge of a strict episcopal hierarchy of Archbishops and Bishops.
p3: All clergy and royal officials had to swear an oath of loyalty to Elizabeth. Parliament tried to enforce capital punishment for refusal → Elizabeth did not enforce this.

front: What were the key provisions of the Act of Uniformity (1559)?
p1: Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer used in all churches — but the 'Black Rubric' explicitly denying Transubstantiation was omitted, leaving the question deliberately ambiguous.
p2: Visitations by bishops to ensure all churches were following the Church of England style as set out in Royal Injunctions.
p3: Everyone must attend a licensed Church of England church on Sundays — recusancy fine of 1 shilling (a labourer's average weekly wage).

front: What did the Royal Injunctions of 1559 establish?
p1: Church taxes (First Fruits and Tenths) paid to the Crown. The small monasteries Mary had managed to restore were dissolved again.
p2: Clergy to wear distinctive vestments. Clergy could marry. Music encouraged at services; images (statues and stained glass) accepted.
p3: Elizabeth described the settlement as Via Media — 'the middle way' — designed to be an acceptable compromise that would end religious conflict.

front: What were Matthew Parker's key actions as Archbishop (1559–75)?
p1: Parker had been Anne Boleyn's chaplain — a Protestant who had not gone into exile during Mary's reign and was not radicalised by Calvinism or Zwinglism.
p2: Defended the Religious Settlement: oversaw passage of the 39 Articles at Convocation 1563, resisting Puritan attempts to introduce more radical changes — defeated by a single vote.
p3: Reached compromise with Puritans during the Vestiarian Controversy in his 1566 Advertisements — clergy could wear simply a 'comely surplice with long sleeves' at Communion.

front: What were Grindal's and Whitgift's key actions as Archbishop?
p1: Edmund Grindal (1575–83): former Marian exile, sympathetic to Puritan concerns. Came into conflict with Elizabeth over prophesyings — unlicensed meetings where clergy preached and discussed scripture.
p2: Ordered to suppress prophesyings 1576 → refused, writing that he must 'obey God rather than man'. Suspended 1577, confined to house arrest.
p3: Remained suspended until death 1583 — never restored to favour. Showed Elizabeth would tolerate no challenge to her control of the Church, however principled.

front: What were Whitgift's methods as Archbishop (1583–1604)?
p1: John Whitgift used the Court of High Commission to investigate and discipline non-conformist clergy. Required subscription to the Three Articles — swearing Elizabeth's supremacy; exclusive use of the Book of Common Prayer; and that the 39 Articles were scripturally sound.
p2: ~300 Puritan clergy removed or suspended. The anonymous Marprelate Tracts (1588–89) — scurrilous pamphlets attacking bishops — showed Puritan resistance had not been broken.
p3: Elizabeth supported Whitgift fully and died holding his hand — she called him her 'black husband'. Determined repression contained the Puritan challenge without eliminating it.

front: What were the events of the Rising of the North (1569–70)?
p1: Plot to marry Mary to the Duke of Norfolk uncovered. Catholic northern earls of Northumberland and Westmoreland launched an uprising.
p2: Rebels captured Durham — held Catholic Latin mass in the Cathedral. Summons issued to other Catholic nobility and gentry — none answered the call.
p3: Royal army led by the Earl of Sussex marched north → rebels fled without battle. Mary moved to Coventry. Elizabeth executed 450 rebels.

front: What was the significance of Mary Queen of Scots' arrival in England and the Papal Bull of 1570?
p1: Mary QoS forced to abdicate 1567 following suspected involvement in assassination of Lord Darnley. Fled to northern England 1568 → placed under house arrest.
p2: A real danger: Elizabeth's cousin; next in line; if she succeeded she would likely restore Catholicism. Presence in the highly Catholic North → a figurehead around which plots would ferment.
p3: 1570: Pope Pius V issued Regnans in Excelsis, excommunicating Elizabeth — Catholics now absolved of loyalty to her → transformed the Catholic threat from passive non-conformity to active potential treachery.

front: What were the three main Catholic plots against Elizabeth?
p1: 1571 Ridolfi Plot: Ridolfi plotted with Pope, Philip II and Duke of Norfolk to marry Mary to Norfolk and provoke a Catholic uprising. Discovered by Cecil. Norfolk executed 1572 — Elizabeth resisted calls to execute Mary.
p2: 1583 Throckmorton Plot: involved Duke of Guise, Philip II and seminary priests. Uncovered by Walsingham → Bond of Association 1584: Privy Council pledged to execute anyone implicated in future plots against Elizabeth.
p3: 1586 Babington Plot: planned Elizabeth's assassination and Spanish-French invasion. Walsingham found evidence directly implicating Mary → Parliament petitioned — Mary executed February 1587.

front: How did the government targeted seminary priests and Jesuits?
p1: Walsingham ran extensive spy networks to track missionary priest networks. Priests tortured until they revealed contacts. Edmund Campion — captured 1581, racked and executed — became the most famous Catholic martyr.
p2: 1581: recusancy fines raised to £20 a month; converting someone to Catholicism made treason. 1585: all Catholic priests expelled from England; harbouring a priest → capital offence.
p3: 133 seminary priests and Jesuits executed. Persecution created martyrs → arguably hardened Catholic resistance. Number of recusants did not significantly decline despite the severity of the laws.

front: How effectively did Elizabeth manage faction on her Privy Council?
p1: Elizabeth stayed aloof — delayed decisions; showed favour to no faction → forced councillors to compete for her approval. Used gender to manage loyalty: courtiers competed for her affection, giving her leverage no male monarch would have had.
p2: 1565–66: Leicester came into dispute with Norfolk and Sussex over Amy Robsart's death — almost ended in violence. Elizabeth resolved it by making clear she would not marry Leicester.
p3: 1578–85: Dutch Revolt divided the Council — Leicester and Walsingham urged intervention; Burghley counselled caution. Elizabeth delayed until assassination of William of Orange 1585 forced her hand.

front: Why did Elizabeth refuse to marry or name a successor?
p1: Resented sharing power — described naming a successor as 'buried alive': enemies would plot around that person; ministers would desert her for the incoming monarch.
p2: Choice almost impossible: foreign monarch risked entanglement (cf. Mary I and Philip); English noble would create faction; almost all candidates were Catholic.
p3: Personal experience coloured her view: her mother executed; stepmother Catherine Howard executed; her sister's marriage brought war and humiliation. Marriage meant danger.

front: What was the impact of Elizabeth's refusal to resolve the succession question?
p1: Bond of Association (1584): Privy Council pledged to kill anyone linked to future plots against Elizabeth. Combined pressure of Lords, Commons and Privy Council after Babington Plot → Mary executed 1587.
p2: Despite never naming a successor, Elizabeth tacitly acknowledged James VI would succeed — managing expectations without the political cost of a formal declaration.
p3: Peaceful succession of James I in 1603 vindicated her strategy of deliberate ambiguity. Cecil had been in secret correspondence with James for years before Elizabeth's death.

front: What were the powers of the Elizabethan monarch?
p1: Monarch derived power directly from God. All legislation required Royal Assent — absolute right to veto.
p2: Could issue Royal Proclamations; could call, prorogue and dissolve Parliament at will. Presided at Court surrounded by courtiers competing for favour.
p3: Royal Prerogative: matters only the monarch could decide — religion; war; succession; foreign policy.

front: What were the roles of the Privy Council and Parliament?
p1: Privy Council: monarch's most important advisors — maximum 20 members, met several times a week. Dominated most of the reign by William Cecil.
p2: Parliament: could pass legislation more permanent than a proclamation. Monarch needed parliamentary approval for taxation. Called only ten times during Elizabeth's reign.
p3: Parliament increasingly claimed the right to debate matters Elizabeth considered part of the Royal Prerogative — religion; marriage; succession. Unresolved tension inherited by the Stuarts.

front: Who was William Cecil and what did he achieve?
p1: Elizabeth's principal advisor until death 1598. Secretary of State until 1572; Lord Treasurer 1572–98. Became Lord Burghley 1571.
p2: Helped draft the Religious Settlement; managed correspondence; created an intelligence service to discover plots; ran the Privy Council.
p3: By nature cautious and pragmatic — prudence often aligned with Elizabeth's instincts on difficult decisions. The most important figure in Elizabethan government.

front: What specific tools and methods did Elizabeth use to control Parliament?
p1: Elizabeth could dissolve a Parliament she disapproved of and call a new one, or prorogue it — suspending proceedings while pressure was applied to MPs.
p2: Elizabeth and the Privy Council influenced choice of Speaker, who controlled debates. Could use Royal Veto if a bill passed both Houses. As a last resort, could arrest MPs as traitors.
p3: Privy Council expected to promote Elizabeth's wishes in Parliament — many Councillors were prominent politicians who dominated parliamentary business.

front: What were the main parliamentary conflicts over religion and freedom of speech?
p1: Catholic Lords and Bishops attempted to block the Act of Supremacy 1559 — defeated after Easter prorogation and suspension of two bishops.
p2: Puritans: Strickland's Bill (1571) and Cope's 'bill and book' (1586) both attempted to alter the Religious Settlement → blocked as infringements of the Royal Prerogative.
p3: Wentworth brothers criticised Elizabeth's denial of Parliament's rights to discuss marriage and succession (1566, 1571, 1576, 1587, 1593). Peter Wentworth 1576: compared Elizabeth to 'the work of the devil' → sent to the Tower by the rest of the House.

front: What were the parliamentary conflicts over marriage and Mary Queen of Scots?
p1: Many MPs feared Elizabeth dying unmarried → throne to the Catholic Mary Queen of Scots. Petitions to marry presented 1559 and 1563.
p2: 1566 Parliament: demand to marry attached to the subsidy bill following Elizabeth's near-fatal smallpox 1562. Elizabeth reduced subsidy by a third but reaffirmed succession as her Royal Prerogative.
p3: Parliament vehemently hostile to Mary QoS, pushed for her execution for years. After Babington Plot, combined pressure of Lords, Commons and Privy Council → Mary executed February 1587.

front: Who were Elizabeth's main suitors?
p1: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester — Elizabeth's likely personal preference. Scandalous choice: his father, brother and grandfather had all been executed as traitors. Amy Robsart's suspicious death 1560 made him unmarriageable in public eyes.
p2: Habsburg candidates: Archduke Charles of Austria — promoted by Cecil 1567, but his insistence on practising Catholicism was a dealbreaker. Philip II proposed 1559 — wildly unpopular after Mary's reign.
p3: Francis, Duke of Alençon — the only suitor to visit in person (1579). Elizabeth genuinely fond of him, calling him her 'frog'. Died 1584 — ending the last serious marriage negotiation.

front: What was the role of gender in Elizabethan government?
p1: Elizabeth used gender as a political tool — courtiers competed for her affection → gave her leverage over faction that a male monarch would not have had.
p2: Gender created real problems: Parliament and Council assumed a queen needed a husband → persistent pressure to marry. Her gender used to justify demands that she name a successor.
p3: Marriage could forge foreign alliances — but any husband risked becoming a co-ruler sharing sovereignty. As Mary I's marriage to Philip proved, a foreign consort caused more problems than the alliance was worth.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What was the financial situation Elizabeth inherited in 1558?
p1: Inherited debt of £227,000 from Mary's war with France, owed to the Antwerp Exchange at 14% interest. Gresham identified three problems: debasement of coinage; cost of war; Hanseatic League control of wool exports.
p2: Gresham's advice: maintain excellent credit rating by repaying debts swiftly and avoiding loans in peacetime → when war came, Elizabeth could borrow quickly at favourable rates.
p3: Mary's revised Book of Rates dramatically boosted customs revenue. Elizabeth retained able administrators in Gresham and Lord Treasurer Paulet — a significant advantage she wisely used.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How successfully did Elizabeth manage the Crown's finances before 1585?
p1: Marian debt effectively removed — by 1576 Chancellor of the Exchequer informed Parliament it had been cleared. By 1584 Elizabeth had accrued a surplus of £300,000.
p2: Achieved by: not indulging in excessive lifestyle; no lavish building projects; going on summer progress at courtiers' expense; avoiding war at all costs.
p3: But sold significant Crown Lands — brought in £600,000 but depleted long-term income. Custom Farmers → widespread corruption. Refused to fund a professional tax-collecting service.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What caused inflation during Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Population rise c.2.7 to c.4 million between 1547 and 1603 → demand outstripped supply. Poor harvests — common due to the Little Ice Age — reduced supply further. By 1560s, average food prices triple those of Henry VII's reign.
p2: Bullion: gold and silver from the New World reduced the value of precious metals across Europe → coinage less valuable, prices rose.
p3: Contemporaries blamed enclosure and greedy landlords — misdiagnosis meant the government could not tackle the underlying cause: rising population affecting supply and demand.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How effectively did overseas trade develop in Europe and the Middle East?
p1: Cloth trade: 75% of exports at start of reign. Dutch Revolt and war with Spain collapsed the Antwerp market → new companies chartered: Muscovy (1555); Eastland (1579); Levant (1580); East India (1600).
p2: Muscovy Company: prosperous — traded cloth for Russian hides. Eastland Company: less successful, struggled against the German Hanseatic League's dominance of the Baltic.
p3: Levant Company (1580): traded with Ottoman Empire, more successful. Overall the new companies partially compensated for the loss of Antwerp but never fully replaced it — cloth exports remained depressed.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How effectively did overseas trade develop in the Americas and Asia?
p1: Americas dominated by Spain and Portugal. Raleigh's colonisation attempts at Roanoke failed in the 1580s. John Dee and Martin Frobisher failed to find a north-west passage.
p2: John Hawkins established English involvement in the Transatlantic Slave Trade (1562) — still dominated by Spanish and Portuguese in this period.
p3: East India Company established 1600 — vital to empire but too early for Elizabeth to benefit. By end of reign, 75% of trade still with traditional European partners.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What caused poverty and vagrancy to grow during Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Growing population (3 to 4 million) → Malthusian Crisis: employers lowered wages while landlords raised rents. Combined with inflation → large amounts of poverty.
p2: Wars with Spain and Ireland compounded the problem — soldiers and sailors discharged far from home, often unpaid and injured → added to the pool of destitute vagrants.
p3: Contemporaries blamed enclosure and greedy landlords. By 1600, over 70% of arable land was enclosed in some areas — but nationally only 2%.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did government attitudes to poverty change at the start Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Distinction made between deserving and undeserving poor. Early legislation only supported the deserving — e.g. 1563 Alms Act created a voluntary poor rate.
p2: Belief that undeserving poor needed regulating, not helping. 1563 Statute of Artificers set maximum wage rates and enforced 7-year apprenticeships. 1572 Vagabonds Act: physical mutilation as punishment for vagrancy.
p3: Poor relief was the domain of the Church, not the state. Early examples are either run at parish level or are voluntary poor rates. JPs took over later in the reign.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did Gresham and Paulet improve royal finances?
p1: Sir Thomas Gresham: highly perceptive financier experienced in key money markets. Stopped debasement → led the recoinage of 1560–61.
p2: 1565: Gresham founded the Royal Exchange as a London equivalent to the Antwerp Exchange. Cecil agreed his argument that relaxing usury laws would stimulate English financial markets.
p3: William Paulet: highly effective Lord Treasurer. Excellent financial management helped Elizabeth clear the Marian debt by 1576.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What were ordinary and extraordinary revenue and how did Elizabeth exploit them?
p1: Ordinary revenue (received annually): Crown lands; Customs Duties; profits from justice; First Fruits and Tenths. Crown land income increased from £86,000 to £111,000 — but significant portions sold.
p2: Customs Duties: Mary's revised Book of Rates dramatically boosted revenue — but not regularly updated → by the 1590s, inflation had significantly eroded its real value.
p3: Extraordinary revenue: parliamentary subsidies (~£100,000) and fifteenths and tenths (~£30,000). Taxes among the lowest in Europe — local gentry systematically undervalued their neighbours' lands.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What were the specific causes of inflation?
p1: Population: rose from c.2.7 to c.4 million between 1547 and 1603. Demand outstripped resources → prices rose. By 1560s, average food prices triple those of Henry VII's reign.
p2: Poor harvests — common due to the Little Ice Age — decreased supply of goods → increased prices.
p3: Bullion: huge quantities of gold and silver from the New World decreased the value of precious metals → coinage became less valuable, prices rose.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did the government attempt to tackle inflation?
p1: Gresham attempted recoinage 1560 — called in debased coins and removed base alloys. By 1561 debased coins called in — but prices did not fall → merchants simply kept the same prices, or higher.
p2: Elizabeth encouraged limiting demand: fasting during Lent; 'fish days' on Wednesdays and Fridays. 1586 Book of Orders prohibited hoarding of grain.
p3: Government could not tackle the issue — did not understand how rising population affected supply and demand. Inflation was a structural problem no Tudor government had the economic tools to solve.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What was the cost of the war with Spain from 1585?
p1: Treaty of Nonsuch: committed Elizabeth to £126,000 per year to support Dutch rebels. Total war cost £4.5 million — £2m Netherlands; £2m Ireland; £500,000 Henry of Navarre; £160,000 defending against the Armada.
p2: Pre-war surplus of £300,000 consumed almost entirely in the first year. Crown land sales accelerated in the 1590s. Elizabeth resorted to monopolies as patronage → price rises and parliamentary dissatisfaction.
p3: War taxation reached unprecedented levels — subsidies approved in 1589 and 1593. Even this insufficient → by end of reign England effectively bankrupt, debts passed to James I.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did the war with Spain disrupt English trade?
p1: Even before 1585, the Dutch Revolt damaged English trade. The 1576 Spanish Fury — mutiny of unpaid Spanish troops — destroyed much of Antwerp, centre of the English wool trade.
p2: Elizabeth's seizure of the Genoese Leon 1568 → Spanish trade embargo until 1573. Outbreak of open war 1585 → closed Spanish and Portuguese markets entirely.
p3: Privateering licences offered some compensation — Drake's circumnavigation (1577–80) returned £600,000 of plunder. East India Company (1600) grew partly from the need to find alternative markets.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What economic benefits did the war with Spain bring?
p1: Flemings fled the Netherlands 1566 — brought improved cloth-making skills to England. French Huguenots fleeing persecution also brought manufacturing skills and trade.
p2: Elizabeth's sponsorship of privateers brought dividends — Drake's circumnavigation (1577–80) stole £400,000 from Spanish ships and ports. His 1587 raid on Cadiz brought £140,000.
p3: Cost of war → Elizabeth resorted to monopolies to reward courtiers → contributed to price rises and dissatisfaction. Crown lands sold in the 1590s further weakened long-term royal finances.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did government attitudes to poverty shift in Elizabeth's later reign?
p1: 1576 Act for the Relief of the Poor: 'able-bodied' poor provided work, often in a House of Correction — first recognition that even the 'undeserving poor' required help, not just punishment.
p2: 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor: begging forbidden; JPs to appoint materials to employ the able-bodied. 1598 Act for Punishment of Rogues: 'sturdy beggars' whipped and returned to their parish of birth.
p3: 1601 Poor Law: state assumed responsibility for the Poor Rate from the Church. 'Deserving' and 'undeserving' poor distinction codified — framework for English poor relief until the 19th century.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What local responses to poverty existed and how effective were they?
p1: Norwich — influenced by experience of Kett's Rebellion — banned begging. Wealthiest citizens contributed regularly to a fund to support the poorest.
p2: Ipswich, Exeter and Cambridge introduced similar schemes. Many wealthy individuals bequeathed funds for the poor in their wills.
p3: Archbishops Parker and Whitgift contributed to almshouses; Leicester established a hospital for the poor in Warwick. Ultimately limited — no replacement for effective central legislation.

front: What was the financial impact of the war with Spain?
p1: £4.5 million cost destroyed Elizabeth's surplus almost immediately. Forced to sell Crown lands and resort to monopolies as patronage → price rises and parliamentary dissatisfaction.
p2: Increased need for taxation — Parliament willing to provide. Double subsidy granted 1589; triple subsidy secured by Burghley 1593.
p3: Victory against the Armada came at huge immediate cost — forced loans of £75,000 from the nobility and £56,000 from the City of London.

front: How effectively did the government respond to the socioeconomic crisis of the 1590s?
p1: Oxfordshire Rising 1596 — protest against enclosure at peak of food crisis. Quickly suppressed. Five ringleaders executed. In the end, only four people actually turned up.
p2: 1597 Tillage Act reversed enclosure carried out since 1588. 1601 Poor Law codified the distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor — made the state permanently responsible for poor relief.
p3: Crisis revealed the structural limits of Elizabethan government — it could respond to disorder but not prevent its underlying causes.

front: What were the key events of the Spanish Armada (1588)?
p1: Philip II sent 130 ships and 57,000 men. English fireships scattered the Armada at Calais. Battle of Gravelines inflicted significant Spanish losses.
p2: Storms destroyed over half the remaining fleet off Scotland and Ireland. Major propaganda triumph — Elizabeth promoted the medal 'God blew, and they were scattered'.
p3: Tilbury speech: 'I know I have the body of a weak, feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king.' Performance as much as reality — the threat was already receding when she spoke.

front: What happened in the war with Spain after the Armada?
p1: At sea, failure common after 1588 — Drake's 'English Armada' 1589 was an unmitigated disaster. English attempts to capture the treasure fleet routinely failed.
p2: Capture of the Madre de Dios 1592 → brought riches worth half the Crown's usual annual income. English support for Dutch rebels ensured their survival and eventual success.
p3: Henry of Navarre's coronation as Henry IV 1589 seemed a huge opportunity — Elizabeth sent £20,000 and 10,000 troops. But his conversion to Catholicism and unilateral peace with Spain 1598 → negated these gains.

front: What were the key issues in Parliament during Elizabeth's later years — monopolies and purveyance?
p1: Monopolies: Elizabeth lacked funds to reward favourites → resorted to granting monopolies (sole right to sell a particular good in England). Raised as a major issue in the Parliament of 1597.
p2: 1601 Parliament: MPs publicly listed monopolies granted since 1597 — including salt, starch, iron and vinegar. Elizabeth annulled the most contentious and delivered the Golden Speech → MPs left satisfied.
p3: Purveyance — monarch's customary right to purchase goods at below market value — criticised by MPs 1589 and 1593. Burghley defended as Royal Prerogative. Elizabeth agreed to investigate abuses but made no major concessions.

front: What was the purveyance dispute in Parliament?
p1: Peter Wentworth MP wrote a pamphlet calling on Parliament to examine candidates for succession. Questioned by the Privy Council 1591; sent to the Tower 1593 — where he stayed until death 1596.
p2: Five of Elizabeth's ten Parliaments were called after 1585 — the war with Spain forced reliance on parliamentary subsidies.
p3: War provided a common enemy around which Crown and Parliament united. Double subsidy granted 1589. Burghley secured a triple subsidy 1593.

front: What were the key parliamentary issues in the later years — succession and taxation?
p1: English Crown had claimed Ireland since the 12th century — but by the 16th century English power truly felt only in the Pale around Dublin.
p2: Ulster and Connaught (north/west): ruled by Gaelic chieftains, opposed to English culture. Munster and Leinster (south/east): ruled by Anglo-Norman families who resented London. All Catholic.
p3: Ireland a persistent source of unrest — Fitzgerald Rebellions 1569–73 and 1579–83. Plantations in Munster attempted to increase control → unsuccessfully.

front: What was the background to Ireland and what caused Tyrone's Rebellion?
p1: 1594: Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, led rebellion of Gaelic chieftains against English rule. Victory at Yellow Ford 1598 — the worst English defeat in Ireland — left Tyrone controlling most of the island.
p2: Essex sent 1599 with 17,000 men — the largest force Elizabeth ever dispatched. Failed disastrously: made an unauthorised truce with Tyrone; returned to London without permission and in disgrace. 4,000 Spanish troops landed at Kinsale 1600 to support Tyrone.
p3: Lord Mountjoy defeated the Spanish at Kinsale 1601 and secured Tyrone's surrender 1603 — just days after Elizabeth's death. War cost ~£2 million → nearly broke Elizabethan finances.

front: What happened during the Nine Years' War?
p1: Rebellion extremely costly to suppress — over £2 million. Crippling in context of war with Spain. Yellow Ford defeat was a humiliation.
p2: 1599: Essex led 16,000 men — the largest force ever sent to Ireland. Returned home without orders, without fighting a battle.
p3: Tyrone's ultimate defeat by Mountjoy secured Ireland → Gaelic lords fled; Protestant plantations in Ulster. England never seriously threatened.

front: How serious a problem was Tyrone's Rebellion?
p1: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex — godson of Leicester, married Walsingham's daughter. Wit, eloquence and dashing personality made him a favourite of the ageing Elizabeth in the 1590s.
p2: Raised to the Privy Council 1593 more for personality than political skill. Arrogance clashed repeatedly with the pragmatic Robert Cecil.
p3: Frequently acted without authorisation: joined Drake's English Armada 1589 against direct orders; disobeyed orders in France 1592. His burning of Cadiz 1596 made him enormously popular across England.

front: What were the specific events of Essex's rise?
p1: In the 1590s, Essex jealous of loss of power. Initially refused to go to Ireland on Elizabeth's orders before being slapped — and half drawing his sword.
p2: In Ireland 1599, led 16,000 men but never fought a battle; returned to London without permission. Defiant return enraged Elizabeth → placed under house arrest.
p3: Under house arrest, Essex lost his monopoly over sweet wines. Mountjoy's success in crushing the Tyrone Rebellion further disgraced him. In desperation → Essex began his 1601 rebellion.

front: What led to Essex's downfall and rebellion?
p1: Essex wrote to James VI warning Robert Cecil would prevent his succession. Commissioned performance of the banned play Richard II — in which a childless monarch is deposed by a nobleman.
p2: Gathered supporters including the Earl of Southampton; marched into the City of London hoping to raise citizens against Cecil. Most supporters got cold feet → rebellion collapsed as Tower's guns turned on Essex House.
p3: Essex and five supporters executed February 1601. Cecil's faction controlled government unopposed from then on → engineered the smooth succession of James I in 1603.

front: What were the key events and consequences of Essex's Rebellion?
p1: Bad harvests 1594–98 → average price of wheat doubled. Cheaper grains rose even faster, hitting the poorest hardest. At the crisis peak 1595–97, the death rate increased by 50%.
p2: Population growth throughout the century had outstripped food supply — a Malthusian Crisis. Collapse of trade due to war with Spain → reduced supply of imported goods and cost jobs in cloth manufacture.
p3: War taxation (unprecedented subsidies 1589 and 1593) and Elizabeth's granting of monopolies further raised prices on staple goods. The 1590s crisis combined natural, economic and fiscal pressures simultaneously.

front: What were the specific causes of the 1590s socioeconomic crisis?
p1: As Elizabeth entered her 60s, looks diminished — blackened teeth; bright red wig; pockmarked face made up with white lead. On progress, public described her as 'old and ill'.
p2: 1596: Privy Council ordered destruction of any 'unseemly and improper' portraits → all portraits had to be based on an agreed flattering version produced by Nicholas Hilliard.
p3: Rainbow Portrait used heavy symbolism: holds a rainbow (peace and divine favour); dress covered with eyes and ears — Elizabeth sees and hears all; no one can plot against her.

front: How did Elizabeth manage her public image in her later years?
p1: Series of scandals undermined Elizabeth's image at court (e.g. Raleigh and Bess Throckmorton's child). Attendance at court decreased; nobility reluctant to accompany her on progress.
p2: Every year on 17 November, Accession Day Tilts lavishly celebrated. Festivals encouraged among ordinary people on Accession Day → celebrate Elizabeth as saviour of England and Protestantism.
p3: Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene glorified Elizabeth as 'Gloriana' — the cult of the Virgin Queen wedded to England was popularised. Reinforced by the 1601 Golden Speech.

front: How did Elizabeth manage her reputation at court in her later years?
p1: Privy Council: monarch's most important advisors — maximum 20 members, met several times a week. Dominated most of the reign by William Cecil. Key function: advising on policy and implementing decisions.
p2: Parliament: could pass legislation more permanent than a proclamation. Monarch needed parliamentary approval for taxation. Called only ten times during Elizabeth's reign.
p3: Parliament increasingly claimed the right to debate matters Elizabeth considered part of the Royal Prerogative — religion; marriage; succession. Unresolved tension inherited by the Stuarts.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was communism?
p1: Marx and Engels: the proletariat (workers) would overthrow capitalism → classless, equal society with no private property.
p2: Lenin adapted Marx's ideas for Russia, founded the Bolshevik Party 1903, seized power October 1917. USSR: one-party authoritarian state.
p3: Marxism-Leninism opposed: religion ('opium of the masses'), private property, parliamentary democracy — dismissed as a camouflage for capitalism.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was capitalism and how did it differ from communism?
p1: Capitalism: private ownership, investment and profit. People produce what the market demands — not what the state directs.
p2: The West believed in: individual liberty, freedom of speech, elected government accountable to the people.
p3: Communism promised economic equality; capitalism produced political freedom but economic inequality — the core ideological clash of the Cold War.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: Why were there long-term tensions between the USSR and the West before 1941?
p1: Bolshevik Revolution 1917 alarmed the West — Britain, USA, France and Japan all intervened in the Russian Civil War (1917–22) on the side of the Whites.
p2: Comintern (1919) confirmed Western fears the USSR sought to export revolution. Stalin's 1930s show trials reinforced Western image of a brutal dictatorship.
p3: Nazi-Soviet Pact (1939) shocked the West — communism and fascism temporarily allied. Munich (1938) convinced Stalin the West wanted Germany and the USSR to destroy each other.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was the Atlantic Charter and why was it significant?
p1: Joint British-American document (August 1941): affirmed self-determination, political freedom and freedom of speech — directly threatening Soviet values.
p2: USSR endorsed it alongside 125 nations January 1942 but played no part in drafting it. Stalin resented being presented with Western values as a condition of alliance.
p3: Demonstrated the fundamental incompatibility of Western and Soviet war aims — the West fought for liberal democracy; the USSR sought a buffer zone of compliant states.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was the second front dispute and why did it cause tension?
p1: USSR proposed the Allies open a second front through France — Stalin felt he was fighting the bulk of the war alone while the West operated in North Africa.
p2: Britain and USA delayed until June 1944. Churchill wanted it in the Balkans to limit Soviet influence — Stalin believed the delay was deliberate.
p3: Soviet FM Gromyko: 'The Cold War began as a secret Cold War when the Allies delayed the second front.' The delay hardened Stalin's suspicion of Western intentions.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: Why was Poland such a divisive issue in the Grand Alliance?
p1: Britain had gone to war to defend Polish independence — the government in exile was hosted in London. Abandoning Poland would be a betrayal.
p2: USSR had invaded eastern Poland 1939 under the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Wanted a 'friendly' (communist) government as a buffer zone — invaded via Poland three times.
p3: Poland symbolised the fundamental clash of war aims: West wanted self-determination and free elections; USSR wanted security through compliant neighbours.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was the Percentages Agreement (1944)?
p1: October 1944: Churchill brokered a secret deal with Stalin dividing Eastern Europe — Romania 90% Soviet, Greece 90% British, Hungary and Yugoslavia 50/50.
p2: Churchill scribbled the percentages on a piece of paper and pushed it to Stalin, who ticked it. Churchill called it a 'naughty document'.
p3: Never formally enacted — USA would not have agreed. Revealed Churchill and Stalin were already dividing Europe, undermining later Western claims to be fighting for self-determination.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was agreed at the Tehran Conference (1943)?
p1: First meeting of the Big Three (Stalin, Roosevelt, Churchill). USA and UK promised to open a second front — D-Day in May/June 1944.
p2: Stalin agreed to declare war on Japan once Germany was defeated.
p3: Vague agreement Germany would remain weak. Most cooperative of the three wartime conferences — the common enemy still dominated.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was agreed at the Yalta Conference (February 1945)?
p1: Germany: divided into four occupation zones; $20 billion in reparations (half to USSR). United Nations to be established.
p2: Stalin promised free elections in Eastern Europe. Eastern Europe acknowledged as a Soviet 'sphere of influence' — never clearly defined.
p3: Poland disputed: Stalin wanted the communist Lublin Committee; Britain hosted the government in exile. Vague language contained the seeds of future conflict.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: What was contested at the Potsdam Conference (July–August 1945)?
p1: West opposed harsh reparations — feared a repeat of Versailles. Stalin (25 million Soviet dead) demanded the most severe terms. No agreement reached.
p2: Between Yalta and Potsdam, Stalin installed a communist puppet government in Poland — Truman strongly objected to this breach of the Yalta agreements.
p3: Truman informed Stalin of the atomic bomb. Bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki without telling him — Stalin saw this as a direct threat.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
front: How did the liberation of Europe differ between East and West?
p1: Western liberation: Allied forces seen as liberators — brought supplies, not annexing territory or imposing ideology.
p2: Eastern liberation: Red Army inflicted harsh retribution — mass reprisals, widespread plunder, deportation of ethnic Germans, annexation of pre-1918 Russian territories.
p3: Soviet political influence spread rapidly: communist coups in Romania (1945), communist-dominated coalitions in Hungary and Bulgaria, pro-Soviet committees in Poland. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia absorbed into USSR.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the role of the United Nations at the start of the Cold War?
p1: Established October 1945, replacing the League of Nations. Security Council: five permanent members (USA, USSR, UK, France, China) each with the power of veto.
p2: At its first meeting 1946, Russia used the veto to block Anglo-French withdrawal from Syria and Lebanon. USA proposed international control of atomic weapons — USSR rejected it.
p3: Despite tensions, the UN provided a diplomatic forum. Korean War (1950–53): USSR was boycotting the Security Council → USA secured a resolution authorising military action.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What did Churchill say in his Iron Curtain speech (March 1946)?
p1: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the continent.' Delivered at Fulton, Missouri with Truman present.
p2: Churchill called for an Anglo-American alliance — Stalin admired strength and despised weakness. The West must negotiate from a position of strength.
p3: Stalin accused Churchill of being 'a firebrand of war'. Despite inaccuracies (Soviet control was not yet complete), the speech hardened attitudes and made the Cold War visible to ordinary people.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What were salami tactics?
p1: USSR's method of taking control of Eastern European governments — entering coalition governments, then 'slicing out' opposition parties one by one.
p2: Methods: rigged elections using violence and intimidation; forced mergers of socialist and communist parties; arrests and murder of opposition leaders; secret police.
p3: By 1948 pro-Moscow communist leaders established across Eastern Europe and all opposition destroyed. Term coined by Hungarian communist Mátyás Rákosi.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: How did the USSR take control of Poland and Czechoslovakia?
p1: Poland: Soviet forces set up Provisional Government June 1945, dominated by communists. By January 1947 rigged elections gave communists 80% of the vote under Gomulka.
p2: Czechoslovakia: free elections 1946 gave communists only 38%. February 1948: communist coup — foreign minister Jan Masaryk was defenestrated.
p3: Czech coup shocked the West — played on guilt (Britain had failed to stop Hitler taking Czechoslovakia in 1938–9) and directly accelerated the formation of NATO.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Long Telegram and the Novikov Telegram?
p1: Long Telegram (February 1946): George Kennan, US ambassador in Moscow, argued Stalin sought destruction of capitalism — but was not suicidal and would back down under pressure.
p2: Novikov Telegram (September 1946): Soviet ambassador in Washington reported the USA planned to dominate the world using its military might — cooperation since Roosevelt's death was impossible.
p3: Both confirmed to each side that the other was their enemy. The Long Telegram became the intellectual basis for containment — firm pressure would make the Soviets back down.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Truman Doctrine?
p1: 12 March 1947: Truman appealed to Congress to support free peoples resisting subjugation. Committed $400 million to anti-communist fighters in Greece and Turkey.
p2: Triggered by Britain's announcement it could no longer fund anti-communist forces in Greece. By 1947 Stalin was breaking his Yalta promises about free elections in Eastern Europe.
p3: Deliberately broad — committing America not just to Greece but to opposing communist expansion anywhere in the world. End of US isolationism.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Marshall Plan?
p1: June 1947: Secretary of State George Marshall offered $13 billion in aid to Europe. No distinction between 'free' and 'unfree' countries — but Stalin forbade satellite states to attend the Paris meeting.
p2: 16 nations attended without the Soviet bloc. Aid funded re-industrialisation of West Germany and promoted stability — preventing desperation from driving countries towards communism.
p3: Stalin called it 'Dollar Imperialism'. Tightened control of Eastern Europe in response → created Cominform (1947) and Comecon (1949). Europe now split into two economic blocs.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What were Cominform and Comecon?
p1: Cominform (September 1947): Stalin's response to the Truman Doctrine — coordinated all European communist parties, directed satellite leaders to follow the Moscow line. Yugoslavia expelled 1948 for resisting Soviet control.
p2: Comecon (1949): economic counterpart to the Marshall Plan. Bound Eastern European economies to the USSR — traded on terms favourable to Moscow, providing markets and raw materials for Soviet industry.
p3: Together they tightened Soviet political and economic control — preventing satellite states from trading freely with the West or developing independent foreign policies.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What caused the Berlin Blockade?
p1: Germany divided into four occupation zones. West wanted Germany to recover as a buffer; USSR wanted reparations and a weak Germany. Bizonia (1947) combined US and British zones.
p2: June 1948: West introduced the Deutschmark without consulting the USSR — Stalin's key aim was to prevent a West German state.
p3: 23 June 1948: Stalin cut all road and rail links to West Berlin and switched off its electricity — squeezing the West's most vulnerable point, 110 miles inside the Soviet zone.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What happened during the Berlin Airlift and what were its consequences?
p1: Western planes supplied the city entirely by air — Stalin could not shoot them down without starting a war. Daily tonnage reached 8,000 tonnes by February 1949. Stalin lifted the blockade May 1949.
p2: Propaganda disaster for the USSR — confirmed the image of Soviet aggression. Directly accelerated the formation of NATO (April 1949).
p3: Led to two separate German states: Federal Republic of Germany (West, May 1949) and German Democratic Republic (East, October 1949).

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the East German Rising of 1953?
p1: Ulbricht imposed harsh economic policies — high production quotas, low wages, collectivisation. 16–17 June 1953: workers in East Berlin struck; protests spread to over 400 towns, ~400,000 participants.
p2: Demands became political: free elections and end of the SED regime. Soviet tanks deployed 17 June. ~55 killed, 20 executed, thousands arrested. Crushed within days.
p3: Showed communism's shallow roots in the DDR — workers rising against a workers' state. In West Germany, 17 June became the national holiday 'Tag der Deutschen Einheit' until reunification 1990.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was NATO and why was it created?
p1: North Atlantic Treaty (4 April 1949): formed after the Berlin Blockade and Czech coup. Article 5 — an attack on one member is an attack on all.
p2: Committed America permanently to European defence, reversing pre-war isolationism. US military bases established across Western Europe.
p3: NATO expanded as threats grew: USSR tested atomic bomb (1949), North Korea invaded South Korea (1950), permanent Paris HQ established 1952 with 35 divisions. West Germany joined May 1955.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Warsaw Pact and why was it created?
p1: Signed 14 May 1955 — one week after West Germany joined NATO. USSR and most Eastern European satellites. A direct Soviet response to West German rearmament.
p2: Unlike NATO, not a genuine alliance of independent states — the USSR already controlled members' foreign and defence policies. Gave legal framework for stationing Soviet troops in Eastern Europe.
p3: A clause stated it would lapse if a 'general European treaty of Collective Security' were signed — more political than defensive. Suppression of dissent could now be labelled 'Warsaw Pact action'.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: How did the arms race develop between 1945 and 1955?
p1: USA bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki August 1945. Stalin accelerated the Soviet programme — aided by Klaus Fuchs, who passed Manhattan Project designs to the USSR. Soviets tested first atomic bomb 1949, years earlier than expected.
p2: USA tested hydrogen bomb 1952 (1,000 times more powerful); USSR tested its own 1953. Both sides developed ICBMs in 1957. Rosenbergs executed June 1953 for passing atomic secrets to Moscow.
p3: Led to Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) — any nuclear strike would be met by devastating retaliation, making nuclear war suicidal for both sides.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was the Doctrine of Massive Retaliation (1954)?
p1: John Foster Dulles, Eisenhower's Secretary of State: the USA would respond to Soviet aggression anywhere with an overwhelming nuclear strike. Part of Eisenhower's 'New Look' — nuclear weapons cheaper than conventional armies.
p2: Response to the Korean War — conventional deterrence proved expensive and inconclusive. Nuclear weapons offered 'more bang for the buck'.
p3: Became less credible as Soviet nuclear capability grew — threatening total war over a limited Soviet move looked reckless. Replaced by Kennedy's 'flexible response' in the 1960s.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
front: What was Stalin's Peace Note (1952) and why was it rejected?
p1: March 1952: Stalin proposed a unified, democratic and neutral Germany — free elections, all occupation forces withdrawn, no alliance obligations. Timed to derail West German rearmament and NATO integration.
p2: West rejected it — feared a reunified Germany would drift Soviet. Adenauer, whose strategy depended on Western alignment, opposed reunification on these terms. West doubted Stalin would deliver genuine free elections.
p3: Historians divided: Wilfried Loth argues it was genuine; Rolf Steininger sees it as propaganda. Rejection is one of the Cold War's great 'what-ifs' — reunification may have been achievable in 1952.

front: What was Khrushchev's secret speech (1956)?
p1: February 1956: Khrushchev denounced Stalin's crimes at the 20th Party Congress — the purges, show trials, cult of personality, abuse of power. Not intended to be made public but quickly leaked.
p2: De-Stalinisation launched: political prisoners released, cult of personality dismantled. Called for 'peaceful co-existence' with the West. Brief reconciliation with Yugoslavia (Belgrade Declaration).
p3: Unintended consequences — raised expectations for reform Khrushchev could not satisfy. Directly triggered the Polish October and Hungarian Uprising of 1956.

front: What was the Polish October (1956)?
p1: Protests began June 1956 at Poznan factories — initially over wages, quickly political. Party liberals refused to accept Moscow's nominee as defence minister.
p2: October 1956: support went to Gomulka — a communist imprisoned 1949–54 for 'deviationism'. Khrushchev accepted Gomulka rather than invade — calculated he was the safer option.
p3: Gomulka proved a limited reformer — loyal to the USSR and Warsaw Pact. Showed Khrushchev would tolerate controlled reform to avoid outright rebellion.

front: What caused the Hungarian Uprising of 1956?
p1: Hungary under Stalinist rule: Rakosi's brutal AVH secret police, collectivisation, Soviet-controlled economy. Khrushchev's secret speech raised hopes for change.
p2: October 1956: police fired on protesters — workers, students and intellectuals joined in. Imre Nagy took power: released political prisoners, ended the one-party state, asked Khrushchev to withdraw Soviet troops. Khrushchev initially accepted.
p3: Nagy went too far — announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact and become neutral. Threatened a chain reaction across the Eastern bloc. Khrushchev ordered the invasion.

front: What happened during the Hungarian Uprising and what were its consequences?
p1: Over 1,000 Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest. 3,000 Hungarians killed; 180,000 fled west. Janos Kadar installed. Nagy fled to the Yugoslav embassy — arrested and executed 1958.
p2: West failed to intervene — Suez Crisis had split the Western alliance. Britain and France had invaded Egypt; America condemned them. Could not denounce Soviet aggression in Hungary while supporting Western imperialism in Egypt. Nasser's role key.
p3: Showed the limits of containment: NATO was defensive and would not enter the Soviet sphere. The Iron Curtain was a reality the West accepted, not merely declared.

front: Why did West Germany rearm and join NATO (1955)?
p1: Korean War showed NATO needed more conventional ground forces. Spofford Compromise (1951–52): limited West German troops under Allied command as an interim measure while the EDC debate continued.
p2: René Pleven proposed the European Defence Community — an integrated European army. France rejected it August 1954. West Germany joined NATO directly May 1955; Bundeswehr barred from nuclear weapons.
p3: Hallstein Doctrine (1955): FRG would break diplomatic relations with any state recognising the GDR. Warsaw Pact signed just days after West Germany joined NATO — a direct Soviet response.

front: What was the Berlin Crisis of 1958–61?
p1: West Berlin: people could still cross freely — 1949–61, ~3.5 million East Germans fled West, including many skilled professionals. Brain drain threatened the DDR's economic survival.
p2: November 1958: Khrushchev issued the Berlin Ultimatum — West had six months to leave West Berlin or he would hand control to East Germany. USA, UK and France refused.
p3: Crisis attempts failed: Paris Summit (1960) collapsed when a U-2 spy plane was shot down over the USSR and Eisenhower refused to apologise. Vienna Summit (1961) failed when Khrushchev tried to bully Kennedy.

front: Why was the Berlin Wall built and why was it significant?
p1: 12–13 August 1961: border sealed overnight with barbed wire; concrete wall with a 'death strip' followed. Families separated without warning. ~5,000 escaped before 1989; others were shot crossing.
p2: Wall ended the brain drain — short-term success for Khrushchev. But a state that needed a wall to stop people leaving had visibly failed. Kennedy visited 1963: 'Ich bin ein Berliner'.
p3: USA condemned it but accepted it rather than risk war — tacitly acknowledging Germany's division as permanent. Wall became the Cold War's defining symbol of repression until November 1989.

front: Why did the Space Race matter?
p1: USSR launched Sputnik (October 1957) — the first satellite, shocking the USA. Showed Soviet rocket technology was ahead; a satellite over the USA could be weaponised.
p2: USSR led: Gagarin first human in space (April 1961). USA formed NASA; Kennedy pledged to reach the moon before 1970. Armstrong and Aldrin landed July 1969.
p3: Space and nuclear rockets shared the same technology — Space Race was the arms race by other means. Apollo-Soyuz mission (1975) symbolised détente.

front: What was the Prague Spring (1968)?
p1: January 1968: Dubček launched 'socialism with a human face' — reduced censorship, released political prisoners, freedom of speech. Alarmed Brezhnev, who feared a chain reaction across the Eastern bloc.
p2: July 1968: USSR and Warsaw Pact states sent the Warsaw Letter — warning the reforms threatened socialism. Dubček refused to reverse them.
p3: August 1968: 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops invaded. Dubček replaced by Gustáv Husák. Jan Palach self-immolated in protest.

front: What were the consequences of the Czech Crisis of 1968?
p1: Brezhnev Doctrine announced: the USSR had the right to intervene if socialism was threatened in any communist state — reform was now off the agenda across the Eastern bloc.
p2: USA did not intervene — too deeply involved in Vietnam. Albania left the Warsaw Pact in protest; Yugoslavia and Romania condemned the invasion and moved closer to China.
p3: Doctrine discouraged reform until Gorbachev abandoned it in 1988. Its abandonment — the Sinatra Doctrine — directly enabled the 1989 revolutions.

front: How did espionage shape the early Cold War?
p1: Klaus Fuchs passed Manhattan Project atomic designs to the Soviets — accelerated their bomb by years. Julius and Ethel Rosenberg (executed 1953) passed related intelligence, inflaming McCarthyism in the USA.
p2: Cambridge Five (Philby, Burgess, Maclean, Blunt, Cairncross): recruited at Cambridge in the 1930s, spied inside British intelligence for decades. Kim Philby — head of MI6's anti-Soviet section — destroyed Western spy networks and alerted Moscow to operations against it. Fled to USSR 1963.
