p3: U-2 spy plane (1960) shot down over the USSR — Eisenhower refused to apologise, wrecking the Paris Summit. Showed how espionage directly destroyed diplomacy.

front: How did espionage shape the later Cold War?
p1: Aldrich Ames (arrested 1994): CIA officer who spied for the Soviet Union from 1985. Revealed virtually every CIA source inside the USSR — at least ten executed. Motivated by money, not ideology.
p2: Gunter Guillaume — personal aide to West German Chancellor Willy Brandt — exposed as an East German Stasi spy in 1974. Forced Brandt to resign, ending the political career of the architect of Ostpolitik.
p3: Espionage was a permanent feature of Cold War relations, demonstrating that even during détente both sides viewed each other as fundamentally hostile.

front: What was Solidarity in Poland (1980–81)?
p1: 1980: workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk struck over food prices. Led by Lech Walesa, they formed Solidarity — the first independent trade union in the Eastern bloc. Quickly grew to 10 million members.
p2: Solidarity demanded: free trade unions, the right to strike, freedom of speech, release of political prisoners. A broad political movement threatening the communist monopoly on power.
p3: December 1981: General Jaruzelski declared martial law — Solidarity banned, Walesa imprisoned. Survived underground; Pope John Paul II (a Pole, elected 1979) crucial in sustaining Polish resolve.

front: Why did the superpowers want détente?
p1: USSR spending ~40% of its budget on defence while economic growth stalled. Sino-Soviet split → armed clashes on the Ussuri River (1969). Desperately needed US grain and technology.
p2: USA weakened by Vietnam, anti-war protests and the 1973 oil crisis. Nixon and Kissinger sought to manage the Soviet threat more cheaply and separate the USSR from China.
p3: Nuclear parity made confrontation too dangerous — by the late 1960s both sides had second-strike capability. Cuban Missile Crisis had shown the risks of brinkmanship.

front: What was SALT I and what were its limitations?
p1: 1972: Nixon and Brezhnev signed the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty — 5-year freeze on missile launcher construction; limits on ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles.
p2: MIRVs (Multiple Independently Targeted Re-entry Vehicles, developed from 1964): one missile could carry warheads aimed at multiple targets — SALT I's freeze on launchers was partly illusory; destructive capacity could still grow.
p3: First formal arms limitation agreement — showed both sides recognised the dangers of the race. Groundwork for Helsinki Accords (1975) and SALT II (1979). Arms race continued in new forms.

front: What were the Helsinki Accords (1975)?
p1: 33 nations agreed three 'baskets': Basket 1 — European borders inviolable; Basket 2 — economic and scientific cooperation; Basket 3 — human rights to be respected. Seen as the zenith of détente.
p2: Basket 3 ignored in practice by the USSR — but gave Eastern European dissidents a legal basis to demand their rights, increasingly important in the 1980s.
p3: Same year: Apollo-Soyuz mission — US and Soviet astronauts shaking hands in orbit, symbolising the spirit of détente.

front: What was Ostpolitik?
p1: Willy Brandt, West German Chancellor from 1969: abandoned the Hallstein Doctrine and normalised relations with the Eastern bloc. Moscow Treaty (1970) — accepted inviolable post-war borders; Warsaw Treaty (1970) — recognised Oder-Neisse line with Poland.
p2: Basic Treaty (1972) — FRG recognised the GDR as a sovereign state; both Germanies joined the UN. West Germany-Czechoslovakia Treaty (1973) revoked the Munich Agreement.
p3: Brandt won Nobel Peace Prize 1971. Resigned 1974 after aide Gunter Guillaume exposed as Stasi spy. Ostpolitik's achievements maintained by subsequent governments.

front: Why did the USSR invade Afghanistan (1979)?
p1: 1978: communist PDPA seized power in Afghanistan. Its atheist policies alienated the Muslim population — religious leaders imprisoned and murdered. Anti-communist Mujahedeen resistance formed.
p2: Brezhnev feared: collapse of the communist government would spread Islamic fundamentalism into the USSR's Central Asian republics; a US-backed state on the Soviet border near the Persian Gulf.
p3: Christmas Day 1979: 100,000 Soviet forces invaded. Killed Afghan leader Amin, installed pro-Moscow Kamal. Red Army ill-prepared for mountain guerrilla warfare. USA's Operation Cyclone supplied Mujahedeen via Pakistan.

front: What were the consequences of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan?
p1: Decade-long guerrilla war the Red Army could not win. Over 38,000 Soviets killed or wounded. Carter cancelled SALT II, imposed sanctions, boycotted 1980 Moscow Olympics. USSR boycotted 1984 Los Angeles Olympics in retaliation.
p2: War eroded Soviet willingness to use military intervention — directly influenced Gorbachev's decision not to use force to maintain communist regimes in 1989.
p3: When glasnost freed the press, Afghanistan's failures became public — fuelling demands for political change. Spiralling costs drained an economy already over-spending on defence.

front: What was the new Cold War (1979–1984)?
p1: Reagan called the USSR an 'evil empire', raised military spending from $171bn (1981) to $376bn (1986). Stationed Pershing and Cruise missiles in Western Europe 1983. KAL 007 shot down by USSR 1983 — 269 killed.
p2: SDI ('Star Wars', 1983): space-based laser system to intercept Soviet ICBMs — threatened to make the entire Soviet nuclear arsenal obsolete.
p3: Able Archer 83: NATO exercise simulating nuclear war — mistaken by USSR for a real strike; Soviet forces went on alert. Most dangerous moment of the new Cold War.

front: How did the new Cold War end and why did the USSR change course?
p1: Internal economic stagnation — not Reagan's military build-up — was the primary driver of Soviet change. USSR over-spending on defence while producing too few consumer goods.
p2: SDI was decisive in bringing Gorbachev to the negotiating table — he concluded the USSR could not win an arms race. Reagan Doctrine: USA funded anti-communist resistance groups worldwide.
p3: Carter Doctrine (1980): USA would respond strongly to any threat to the Persian Gulf — issued after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. SALT II never ratified.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What problems was the USSR facing in the 1980s?
p1: Brezhnev's 'era of stagnation': economy failing; Afghanistan costing vast resources with no results. Chernobyl (1986) exploded — $18 billion spent on containment, exposing industrial inefficiency and corruption.
p2: Poor living standards → unrest in satellite states (e.g. Solidarity in Poland). Reagan's SDI threatened to make Soviet ICBMs obsolete. Andropov and Chernenko — Brezhnev's two elderly successors — meant stagnation at a critical moment.
p3: When Gorbachev became leader 1985, radical change was universally understood to be necessary. USSR over-spending on defence, producing too few consumer goods, losing the technological race.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What were perestroika and glasnost?
p1: Perestroika ('restructuring'): relaxed central control, permitted private enterprise in some industries from 1987. Intended to save the communist system — instead unleashed market forces and expectations the system could not manage.
p2: Glasnost ('openness'): from 1986 media controls relaxed — public learned about government corruption, past crimes, inefficiency. Political prisoners released. Multi-candidate elections introduced from 1987.
p3: Both policies undermined Soviet authority: glasnost exposed the depth of problems; perestroika created disruption without growth. Together they set in motion forces that destroyed the USSR.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: How did Reagan and Gorbachev reduce tensions?
p1: Reykjavik (1986): Gorbachev tried to trade SDI for sweeping arms cuts — Reagan refused. But it produced the INF Treaty (Washington, 1987): total elimination of intermediate-range missiles from Europe. First ever arms reduction agreement.
p2: Reagan and Gorbachev exchanged visits, developed a working relationship. Reagan came to believe Gorbachev was genuinely different from previous Soviet leaders.
p3: Primary driver was Gorbachev's conviction the USSR could not sustain the arms race — Western pressure accelerated his timetable but did not create the necessity.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What was the Sinatra Doctrine?
p1: December 1988: Gorbachev abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine in a speech to the UN — satellite states now free to 'do it their way' (hence 'Sinatra Doctrine').
p2: Single most important decision enabling the 1989 revolutions — removed the threat of Soviet military intervention that had crushed Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968).
p3: By 1989 Gorbachev would not bolster unpopular communist regimes unwilling to reform. Satellite states moved rapidly to exploit the new freedom.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What happened in Poland and Hungary in 1989?
p1: Poland: Round Table Agreements (April 1989) — Solidarity recognised as a party, allowed to contest 35% of parliamentary seats. June 1989 elections: Solidarity landslide — first non-communist government in Eastern Europe since 1948.
p2: Hungary: reformist Imre Pozsgay declared January 1989 the communist monopoly must end. Hungary opened its borders with Austria August 1989 — 150,000 East Germans fled West, triggering the crisis that brought down the Berlin Wall.
p3: Both demonstrated the Sinatra Doctrine was real and that revolutions would not be crushed. Poland's success triggered a wave of revolutions across the Eastern bloc.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: Why did the Berlin Wall fall on 9 November 1989?
p1: Hungary's open border allowed 150,000 East Germans to flee West → mass demonstrations in East German cities, especially Leipzig. Honecker could not count on Soviet support — Gorbachev told him to make changes.
p2: 9 November 1989: government announced East Germans could travel freely. Border guards — overwhelmed by crowds — opened crossings. Crowds demolished the Wall with hammers and pickaxes that night.
p3: Defining symbolic moment of the Cold War's end. Kennedy had pledged 'Ich bin ein Berliner' in 1963 — 26 years later the Wall was gone. Confirmed the Sinatra Doctrine was real.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What happened in Czechoslovakia (1989) and Romania (1989)?
p1: Velvet Revolution (Czechoslovakia): mass demonstrations led by Charter 77 and Vaclav Havel's Civic Forum. Communist Party relinquished power December 1989 — Havel made president. Peaceful, hence 'velvet'.
p2: Romania: the only violent revolution of 1989. Demonstrations in Timisoara spread across the country. Ceausescu and wife fled, were captured and executed 25 December 1989 — the only Eastern European leaders to be killed.
p3: Velvet Divorce (1 January 1993): Czechoslovakia peacefully split into Czech Republic and Slovakia — agreed by Vaclav Klaus and Vladimir Meciar without a referendum.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: How and why was Germany reunified?
p1: Helmut Kohl moved rapidly, fearing the opportunity would close. March 1990: first free elections in East Germany — pro-reunification Alliance for Germany won a clear majority.
p2: 1 July 1990: economic union — Deutschmark replaced East German Mark at 1:1. 3 October 1990: formal reunification. Two Plus Four Treaty with the four wartime Allies settled the borders of the new Germany.
p3: Gorbachev agreed to German NATO membership in exchange for assurances NATO would not expand eastwards — an assurance that became deeply controversial in later decades.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What caused the coup of August 1991 and what were its consequences?
p1: Gorbachev's reforms unleashed forces he could not control. Soviet republics, seeing satellite states gain independence, demanded the same — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence 1990.
p2: August 1991: eight Communist hardliners staged a coup, fearing the imminent Union Treaty would dissolve the USSR. Boris Yeltsin led the resistance — standing on a tank outside parliament, he rallied popular opposition. Coup collapsed in three days.
p3: Christmas Day 1991: Gorbachev resigned and dissolved the USSR. 15 independent states emerged. Russia inherited the UN Security Council seat and nuclear arsenal. USA emerged as the world's sole superpower.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What challenges did Russia face under Yeltsin?
p1: 'Shock therapy' — price controls removed overnight January 1992, causing hyperinflation. State industries privatised corruptly — 'oligarchs' acquired vast assets at far below value.
p2: October 1993: hard-line Communists barricaded the Russian parliament — Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the building, at least 187 killed. December 1994: military campaign in Chechnya produced humiliating defeats.
p3: By the mid-1990s Yeltsin's health was failing and Russia had lost its superpower status. Resigned 31 December 1999, handing power to Vladimir Putin.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
front: What caused the collapse of Yugoslavia?
p1: Tito had kept Yugoslavia independent from the USSR. After his death 1980 the federation fractured. Serbian nationalist Slobodan Milosevic became president 1989 and pressed Serbian interests across Yugoslavia.
p2: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence June 1991 — war broke out immediately. In Bosnia: three-way conflict between Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats. Serbian forces conducted 'ethnic cleansing'. Srebrenica massacre July 1995 — 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys murdered.
p3: NATO bombing 1995 forced the Dayton Peace Agreement. Yugoslavia showed communism had suppressed rather than resolved ethnic nationalism — its removal unleashed catastrophic force.
